title: Be Careful Not to Let Self-Assessments Harm Your Personal Development
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece cautions leaders against treating personality and behavioral assessments like Hogan, DISC, or MBTI as fixed verdicts on who they are. While such tools offer genuine insight into tendencies and preferences, the article argues that people too often use their results as an excuse to stop growing, hiding behind labels like introversion or low agreeableness. The author points to research suggesting personality traits actually shift over time with age and experience, undercutting the idea that self-assessments describe something permanent. The real value of these tools, the piece argues, lies in using them as a starting point for development rather than a ceiling on it. Leaders are urged to keep working on skills like feedback, relationship-building, and decision-making regardless of what a survey says about their natural wiring.
points: Self-assessments reveal genuine tendencies but should not be treated as fixed, unchangeable traits
Using assessment labels as an excuse (e.g., 'I'm an introvert') lets people off the hook for growth
Research shows personality traits evolve with age and experience, contradicting the idea of permanence
The goal of self-assessments should be development, not resignation to a fixed identity
quotes: Rather than appreciating their uniqueness and utilizing the findings of an assessment to make changes, they view the qualities measured as fixed and immutable.
Viewing any proclivity or predisposition as unalterable lets the subject off the hook for becoming the kind of leader and person they can and should become.
Once we see ourselves as having unchangeable qualities and attributes, we naturally give up on trying to change them.
In fact, many of our strongest tendencies evolve as we get older and gain more experience.
Nothing is so fixed or permanent about you that you can’t push beyond your so-called personality and learn how to do things in a more effective way.
It is a tragedy when the results of a self-assessment test rob people of the desire and willingness to do better.
